screens.title: Azure VMs: Your Foundation in IaaS
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Virtual Machines represent a fundamental Infrastructure-as-a-Service, or IaaS, offering. In the IaaS model, Azure provides the virtualized hardware, including compute, storage, and networking, but you, as the developer, retain full responsibility for managing the operating system, runtime, and application layers. This level of control is a key differentiator. For instance, imagine you need to migrate a legacy application that runs on a specific version of Windows Server and requires unique IIS configurations. A VM is the perfect solution because it allows you to replicate that exact environment in the cloud. Similarly, if you're running specialized software that can't be easily containerized or adapted to a serverless model, such as certain database servers or custom enterprise software, VMs provide the necessary flexibility. The misconception here is sometimes thinking IaaS means Azure manages everything; remember, with IaaS, you manage the OS and above, while Azure handles the underlying infrastructure. This balance of control and cloud benefits makes VMs indispensable for many scenarios. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 2.4›Chapter 2.4›Azure VMs: Your Foundation in IaaS
Definition

Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS)

Azure VMs provide virtualized computing resources where Azure manages the underlying hardware, but you manage the operating system, runtime, and applications.

Your Responsibility
  • Operating System (OS) patching and updates
  • Application installation and maintenance
  • Runtime environments and dependencies
  • Data management and security within the OS
Key Takeaway

VMs offer the highest level of control in Azure's compute services, making them ideal for specific migration and software requirements.

Key Scenarios for Azure VMs

Lift-and-Shift Migrations

Migrate existing on-premises applications without significant code changes.

Specialized Software

Run applications requiring specific OS configurations or custom enterprise software.

Legacy Applications

Host older applications that cannot be easily containerized or adapted to serverless.

Specific Database Servers

Deploy database instances requiring dedicated OS control and performance tuning.

screens.title: Provisioning an Azure VM with Azure CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning an Azure VM involves several key decisions and components that define its capabilities and behavior. First, you select an image, which is essentially a template containing the operating system, like Windows Server or Ubuntu. Next, you choose a VM size, which dictates the number of virtual CPUs, memory, and temporary storage available to your VM. This choice directly impacts performance and cost. Networking is another critical component, encompassing the Virtual Network, Subnet, Public IP address for external access, and Network Security Groups to control traffic flow. Finally, you configure storage, including the OS disk where the operating system resides and any additional data disks for your application data. The Azure CLI provides a powerful and scriptable way to manage these components. For example, a simple az vm create command can provision a basic Ubuntu VM, generating SSH keys for secure access and opening port 22 for SSH. This command-line approach allows for automation and consistent deployments, which is vital in a production environment. A common mistake is overlooking the networking configuration, which can lead to connectivity issues or security vulnerabilities if not properly set up.

screens.title: Automating VM Configuration with Extensions
screens.narratorSegment: VM extensions are small applications that run on Azure VMs to provide configuration and automation capabilities immediately after deployment. Think of them as intelligent agents that can perform specific tasks without manual intervention. They are incredibly useful for developers looking to implement infrastructure as code practices, ensuring consistent VM configurations across environments. For example, you can use extensions to install software like a web server, run custom scripts to configure application settings, deploy anti-malware solutions, or collect diagnostics. A particularly powerful type is the custom script extension, which allows you to execute any script—whether it's a Bash script for Linux or a PowerShell script for Windows—directly on your VM. Imagine you've just provisioned a new Ubuntu VM and need to install Nginx and deploy a simple web page. Instead of manually connecting and running commands, you can use a custom script extension to automate this entire setup. This ensures that every VM created with this extension is configured identically, reducing errors and saving significant time. The key takeaway is that extensions transform a raw VM into a fully configured application host automatically.

content.html:
Module 2.4›Chapter 2.4›Automating VM Configuration with Extensions
What are VM Extensions?

Small applications that run on Azure VMs to provide post-deployment configuration and automation capabilities.

Benefits
  • Automate software installation
  • Run custom scripts for setup
  • Configure anti-malware
  • Collect diagnostics
  • Ensure consistent configurations
Key Takeaway

VM extensions are essential for automating setup tasks, enabling infrastructure as code, and ensuring consistent VM deployments.

Custom Script Extension Example
az vm extension set \
  --resource-group MyVmRG \
  --vm-name MyUbuntuVM \
  --name customScript \
  --publisher Microsoft.Azure.Extensions \
  --version 2.1 \
  --settings '{
    "fileUris": ["https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure-Samples/azure-cli-samples/master/vm/install-nginx-on-ubuntu/install-nginx-on-ubuntu.sh"],
    "commandToExecute": "./install-nginx-on-ubuntu.sh"
  }'
Practical Use Case

Automatically install a web server like Nginx and deploy a simple web page immediately after VM creation.

screens.title: Achieving Elasticity with Virtual Machine Scale Sets
screens.narratorSegment: For applications that demand high availability and the ability to scale dynamically, Virtual Machine Scale Sets, or VMSS, are the ideal solution. Instead of managing individual VMs, VMSS allows you to deploy and manage a group of identical, load-balanced virtual machines as a single unit. The real power of VMSS lies in its elasticity: the number of VM instances can automatically increase or decrease in response to real-time demand or a predefined schedule. Imagine a web application that experiences peak traffic during certain hours. With VMSS, you can configure it to automatically scale out, adding more VM instances when C P U usage exceeds a threshold, and then scale back in when demand drops, optimizing costs. This is particularly well-suited for stateless applications, like web servers or A P I backends, where any instance can handle a request. The az vmss create command simplifies the deployment of such a group, allowing you to define the VM image, size, and scaling rules. A common misconception is that VMSS is only for massive scale; it's also excellent for ensuring high availability for even a small number of critical application instances.

Module 2.4›Chapter 2.4›Achieving Elasticity with Virtual Machine Scale Sets
What are VM Scale Sets (VMSS)?

A group of identical, load-balanced VMs that can automatically scale in and out based on demand or a defined schedule.

Key Benefits
  • Automatic Scaling: Adjusts VM count based on metrics.
  • High Availability: Distributes instances across fault domains.
  • Simplified Management: Manage a group as a single resource.
  • Cost Optimization: Scale down during low demand.
Key Takeaway

VMSS provides true elasticity and high availability, making it ideal for stateless applications that need to handle fluctuating loads efficiently.

VMSS Architecture Overview
Load Balancer
Virtual Machine Scale Set
VM Instance 1
VM Instance 2
VM Instance N
Instances automatically scale based on demand (e.g., CPU usage).

screens.title: Securing Azure VM Access and Network Connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: Security for your Azure VMs is absolutely paramount. Always prioritize strong authentication methods: use SSH keys for Linux VMs and robust, complex passwords for Windows VMs. A critical best practice is to avoid exposing management ports, such as port 22 for SSH or port 3389 for RDP, directly to the internet. This creates a significant attack surface. Instead, you should leverage Network Security Groups, or NSGs, which act as a firewall to filter network traffic to and from Azure resources within an Azure Virtual Network. NSGs allow you to define granular rules to restrict inbound and outbound traffic to specific IP addresses, ranges, or service tags. For an even higher level of security and convenience, consider using Azure Bastion. Azure Bastion is a fully managed PaaS service that provides secure and seamless RDP or SSH connectivity to your VMs directly through the Azure portal over TLS, without requiring a public IP on your VMs. This eliminates the need to expose your VMs to the public internet at all for management purposes. Another common mistake is placing sensitive data directly on the OS disk; always use separate, encrypted data disks for application data. By implementing these practices, you significantly enhance the security posture of your Azure VM deployments.

keyIdea.title: Robust VM Security
keyIdea.text: NSGs control traffic, while Azure Bastion provides secure RDP/SSH access without exposing management ports to the internet.

content.html:
Module 2.4›Chapter 2.4›Securing Azure VM Access and Network Connectivity
Core Security Principles
  • Use SSH keys for Linux, strong passwords for Windows.
  • Avoid exposing management ports (22, 3389) directly to the internet.
  • Use separate, encrypted data disks for sensitive application data.
  • Deploy VMs within a Virtual Network (VNet) for private communication.
Common Mistake

Directly exposing RDP/SSH ports to the internet, creating a significant security vulnerability.

Key Security Tools

Network Security Groups (NSG)

Firewall that filters network traffic to and from Azure resources.

Azure Bastion

Secure RDP/SSH connectivity to VMs over TLS, without public IPs.

These tools work together to create a layered security approach for your VMs.

screens.title: Step 1: Provisioning Your Azure VM
screens.narratorSegment: Let's begin our hands-on activity by provisioning an Azure VM. The first crucial step is to create a resource group, which acts as a logical container for all your Azure resources. This helps in organizing and managing your deployments. We'll define a resource group name, such as 'VMDemoRG', and a location, like 'eastus'. Once the resource group is established, we'll proceed to create the Azure VM itself. We'll use the az vm create command, specifying the resource group, a unique VM name like 'MyWebAppVM', and the desired image, in this case, 'UbuntuLTS' for a long-term support Ubuntu server. It's vital to set an admin username, for example, 'azureuser', and to use the --generate-ssh-keys flag. This command automatically creates a public IP address and an associated Network Security Group, and most importantly, generates SSH keys for secure remote access. Remember to note the public IP address from the command output, as you'll need it to connect to your VM later. This initial setup provides a secure and organized foundation for your application deployment. content.html:
Module 2.4›Chapter 2.4›Step 1: Provisioning Your Azure VM
Terminal Demo: Create Resource Group & VM
Command: Create Resource Group
RESOURCE_GROUP="VMDemoRG"
LOCATION="eastus"
VM_NAME="MyWebAppVM"

az group create --name $RESOURCE_GROUP --location $LOCATION

This command creates a new resource group to logically organize your VM and related resources.

Command: Create Azure VM
az vm create \
  --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP \
  --name $VM_NAME \
  --image UbuntuLTS \
  --admin-username azureuser \
  --generate-ssh-keys \
  --public-ip-sku Standard \
  --output json

Creates an Ubuntu VM, generates SSH keys for secure access, and sets up a public IP. Note the publicIpAddress from the output.

Pro-Tip

Always use --generate-ssh-keys for Linux VMs to ensure secure, passwordless authentication, which is a best practice.

screens.title: Step 2: Automating Software Installation with VM Extensions
screens.narratorSegment: Now that our VM is provisioned, let's automate the installation of the Nginx web server using a custom script extension. This is a powerful way to ensure consistent software deployment without manual intervention. First, we'll create a simple Bash script locally, named install underscore nginx. sh. This script will update the package lists, install Nginx, start the Nginx service, enable it to run on boot, and then create a basic 'Hello from Azure VM!' H T M L page. Next, we'll use the az vm extension set command to apply this custom script to our VM. We specify the resource group, VM name, the extension name 'customScript', and its publisher and version. Crucially, we provide the file Uris parameter, pointing to a publicly hosted version of our Nginx installation script. Then, command To Execute tells the extension which command to run on the VM. It's important to note that in a production scenario, you would host your scripts securely in Azure Storage. After executing this command, the extension will download and run the script on your VM, installing Nginx automatically. This demonstrates how extensions streamline post-deployment configuration, saving time and reducing potential errors.

Module 2.4›Chapter 2.4›Step 2: Automating Software Installation with VM Extensions
Terminal Demo: Install Nginx with Custom Script Extension
Script: install_nginx.sh (local creation)
#!/bin/bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nginx
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx
echo "<h1>Hello from Azure VM!</h1>" | sudo tee /var/www/html/index.nginx-debian.html

This script updates packages, installs Nginx, starts it, and creates a simple HTML page.

Command: Apply Custom Script Extension
NGINX_INSTALL_SCRIPT_URL="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure-Samples/azure-cli-samples/master/vm/install-nginx-on-ubuntu/install-nginx-on-ubuntu.sh"

az vm extension set \
  --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP \
  --vm-name $VM_NAME \
  --name customScript \
  --publisher Microsoft.Azure.Extensions \
  --version 2.1 \
  --settings "{\"fileUris\": [\"$NGINX_INSTALL_SCRIPT_URL\"],\"commandToExecute\": \"./install-nginx-on-ubuntu.sh\"}"

This command applies the custom script extension to your VM, executing the Nginx installation script.

Important Note

In a production environment, always host your custom scripts securely in Azure Storage, not a public URL.

screens.title: Step 3: Securing Network Access with NSGs
screens.narratorSegment: With Nginx installed, our next step is to configure the Network Security Group, or NSG, to allow inbound HTTP traffic. By default, when you create a VM with SSH key generation, only port 22 for SSH is open. For our Nginx web server to be accessible from the internet, we need to explicitly open port 80. First, we'll retrieve the name of the NSG associated with our VM using a series of az vm show and az network nic show commands. This ensures we're targeting the correct security group. Once we have the NSG name, we'll use the az network nsg rule create command to add a new inbound security rule. We'll name it 'AllowHTTP', set the protocol to TCP, and specify the destination port range as 80. The priority is important, as lower numbers are processed first; we'll set it to 100. This rule will allow all incoming traffic on port 80, making our Nginx web page accessible. This step highlights the critical role of NSGs in controlling network flow and maintaining a secure posture for your Azure VMs, ensuring only necessary ports are open to the public internet.

keyIdea.title: NSG for Web Access
keyIdea.text: Network Security Groups (NSGs) are crucial for controlling inbound and outbound traffic, allowing specific ports like HTTP (80) while maintaining overall security.

content.html:
Module 2.4›Chapter 2.4›Step 3: Securing Network Access with NSGs
Terminal Demo: Configure NSG for HTTP Traffic
Command: Get NSG Name
NSG_NAME=$(az vm show --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP --name $VM_NAME --query networkProfile.networkInterfaces[0].id --output tsv | xargs -n 1 az network nic show --query networkSecurityGroup.id --output tsv | xargs -n 1 az network nsg show --query name --output tsv)

This command dynamically retrieves the name of the Network Security Group associated with your VM.

Command: Create NSG Rule for HTTP (Port 80)
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP \
  --nsg-name $NSG_NAME \
  --name AllowHTTP \
  --protocol Tcp \
  --direction Inbound \
  --priority 100 \
  --source-address-prefixes '*' \
  --source-port-ranges '*' \
  --destination-address-prefixes '*' \
  --destination-port-ranges 80 \
  --access Allow

This rule opens port 80 (HTTP) for inbound traffic, allowing external access to your Nginx web server.

Security Best Practice

Always apply the principle of least privilege: only open ports that are absolutely necessary for your application to function.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to Chapter 2.4, where we'll dive into Azure Virtual Machines, or VMs. While modern cloud development often highlights serverless and containerized solutions, Azure VMs remain a cornerstone of cloud computing. They fall under the Infrastructure-as-a-Service, or IaaS, category, giving you unparalleled control over the operating system and software stack. This chapter will equip you with the knowledge to understand when VMs are the right choice, how to provision and configure them, and how to manage their scalability and security. We'll explore how VMs are essential for migrating existing on-premises applications, running specialized software, or hosting custom enterprise solutions that demand specific OS configurations. By the end of this chapter, you'll have a solid foundation in deploying and managing robust, controlled compute environments in Azure. Developing Solutions with Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) means azure vms provide foundational iaas capabilities, offering full control over the os and application environment for specific migration and software needs.. In practical terms, mastering iaas for granular control and scalable deployments. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In this chapter, you'll gain practical skills and a deep understanding of Azure Virtual Machines. Our first objective is to help you identify scenarios where Azure VMs are the most appropriate compute choice. This is crucial for making informed architectural decisions, ensuring you select the right tool for the job, whether it's a legacy application migration or a specialized software deployment. You'll learn to recognize the specific requirements that make VMs shine over other Azure compute options. Our second objective focuses on hands-on proficiency: you will learn to provision and configure an Azure VM using the Azure CLI. This command-line interface is a powerful tool for automating deployments and managing your Azure resources efficiently. Mastering these initial steps will lay the groundwork for more advanced VM management and development tasks.

Building on our foundational knowledge, our third objective is to understand VM extensions and how they automate post-deployment configuration. Extensions are powerful tools that allow you to run scripts, install software, or collect diagnostics automatically after your VM is created, significantly streamlining your deployment process and ensuring consistency. Next, you'll learn to implement scaling for VMs using Virtual Machine Scale Sets. This is crucial for building highly available and elastic applications that can automatically adjust to varying user loads, ensuring optimal performance and cost efficiency. Finally, we'll cover how to secure VM access and manage network connectivity. This objective is paramount for protecting your applications and data from unauthorized access, covering best practices for network security groups and secure remote access solutions like Azure Bastion. Together, these objectives will provide a comprehensive understanding of developing robust solutions with Azure VMs.

Azure Virtual Machines represent a fundamental Infrastructure-as-a-Service, or IaaS, offering. In the IaaS model, Azure provides the virtualized hardware, including compute, storage, and networking, but you, as the developer, retain full responsibility for managing the operating system, runtime, and application layers. This level of control is a key differentiator. For instance, imagine you need to migrate a legacy application that runs on a specific version of Windows Server and requires unique IIS configurations. A VM is the perfect solution because it allows you to replicate that exact environment in the cloud. Similarly, if you're running specialized software that can't be easily containerized or adapted to a serverless model, such as certain database servers or custom enterprise software, VMs provide the necessary flexibility. The misconception here is sometimes thinking IaaS means Azure manages everything; remember, with IaaS, you manage the OS and above, while Azure handles the underlying infrastructure. This balance of control and cloud benefits makes VMs indispensable for many scenarios. Azure VMs: Your Foundation in IaaS means azure vms offer iaas, giving full control over the os and application environment, crucial for specific migration and software needs.. In practical terms, granular control over your operating system and software stack.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Provisioning an Azure VM involves several key decisions and components that define its capabilities and behavior. First, you select an image, which is essentially a template containing the operating system, like Windows Server or Ubuntu. Next, you choose a VM size, which dictates the number of virtual CPUs, memory, and temporary storage available to your VM. This choice directly impacts performance and cost. Networking is another critical component, encompassing the Virtual Network, Subnet, Public IP address for external access, and Network Security Groups to control traffic flow. Finally, you configure storage, including the OS disk where the operating system resides and any additional data disks for your application data. The Azure CLI provides a powerful and scriptable way to manage these components. For example, a simple az vm create command can provision a basic Ubuntu VM, generating SSH keys for secure access and opening port 22 for SSH. This command-line approach allows for automation and consistent deployments, which is vital in a production environment. A common mistake is overlooking the networking configuration, which can lead to connectivity issues or security vulnerabilities if not properly set up.

VM extensions are small applications that run on Azure VMs to provide configuration and automation capabilities immediately after deployment. Think of them as intelligent agents that can perform specific tasks without manual intervention. They are incredibly useful for developers looking to implement infrastructure as code practices, ensuring consistent VM configurations across environments. For example, you can use extensions to install software like a web server, run custom scripts to configure application settings, deploy anti-malware solutions, or collect diagnostics. A particularly powerful type is the custom script extension, which allows you to execute any script—whether it's a Bash script for Linux or a PowerShell script for Windows—directly on your VM. Imagine you've just provisioned a new Ubuntu VM and need to install Nginx and deploy a simple web page. Instead of manually connecting and running commands, you can use a custom script extension to automate this entire setup. This ensures that every VM created with this extension is configured identically, reducing errors and saving significant time. The key takeaway is that extensions transform a raw VM into a fully configured application host automatically.

For applications that demand high availability and the ability to scale dynamically, Virtual Machine Scale Sets, or VMSS, are the ideal solution. Instead of managing individual VMs, VMSS allows you to deploy and manage a group of identical, load-balanced virtual machines as a single unit. The real power of VMSS lies in its elasticity: the number of VM instances can automatically increase or decrease in response to real-time demand or a predefined schedule. Imagine a web application that experiences peak traffic during certain hours. With VMSS, you can configure it to automatically scale out, adding more VM instances when C P U usage exceeds a threshold, and then scale back in when demand drops, optimizing costs. This is particularly well-suited for stateless applications, like web servers or A P I backends, where any instance can handle a request. The az vmss create command simplifies the deployment of such a group, allowing you to define the VM image, size, and scaling rules. A common misconception is that VMSS is only for massive scale; it's also excellent for ensuring high availability for even a small number of critical application instances.

Security for your Azure VMs is absolutely paramount. Always prioritize strong authentication methods: use SSH keys for Linux VMs and robust, complex passwords for Windows VMs. A critical best practice is to avoid exposing management ports, such as port 22 for SSH or port 3389 for RDP, directly to the internet. This creates a significant attack surface. Instead, you should leverage Network Security Groups, or NSGs, which act as a firewall to filter network traffic to and from Azure resources within an Azure Virtual Network. NSGs allow you to define granular rules to restrict inbound and outbound traffic to specific IP addresses, ranges, or service tags. For an even higher level of security and convenience, consider using Azure Bastion. Azure Bastion is a fully managed PaaS service that provides secure and seamless RDP or SSH connectivity to your VMs directly through the Azure portal over TLS, without requiring a public IP on your VMs. This eliminates the need to expose your VMs to the public internet at all for management purposes. Another common mistake is placing sensitive data directly on the OS disk; always use separate, encrypted data disks for application data. By implementing these practices, you significantly enhance the security posture of your Azure VM deployments.
